narrationScript: When choosing benchmarks, architects face a fundamental trade-off: synthetic versus real-world benchmarks. Synthetic benchmarks, like Dhrystone or Whetstone, are small, focused kernels designed to test very specific aspects of a processor. They are easy to run and control, making them useful for isolating particular performance characteristics. However, their main limitation is that they often aren't representative of actual complex workloads. Dhrystone, for example, was criticized for being too small to adequately stress modern caches or branch predictors. On the other hand, real-world benchmarks, such as the applications in SPEC or MLPerf, are actual, full-fledged programs. They are highly representative of real usage patterns, but they are also complex, resource-intensive, and more difficult to run and analyze. To bridge this gap and gain highly accurate insights without running full applications repeatedly, architects sometimes use trace-driven simulation. This involves recording detailed instruction traces from real workloads and then feeding these traces into an architectural simulator. It offers high accuracy but generates very large trace files, making it resource-intensive for long runs. Understanding these different approaches helps us evaluate processor performance more critically and make informed architectural decisions.
